claims.text: The starting composite contains isolated W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
Conventional processing of the W–Cu composite produces phase separation and voids at W/Cu interfaces.
Adding 1–3 wt% Ni during rapid ultrahigh-temperature sintering will produce a transient liquid phase at the W/Cu interface.
Transient liquid-phase-assisted rapid sintering can improve bonding between otherwise difficult-to-consolidate composite constituents.
Processing will form a thin, continuous Ni-rich interfacial layer or intermetallic phase at the W/Cu interface.
The Ni-rich interfacial layer will form in situ through interdiffusion.
The Ni-induced transient liquid will enhance wetting and diffusion at the W/Cu interface.
Enhanced interfacial wetting and diffusion will eliminate voids and suppress W–Cu phase separation.
Upon cooling, the interfacial phase will solidify into a defect-minimized, chemically bonded bridge.
A Ni-containing interfacial modification can improve interfacial integrity relative to an unmodified composite.
The chemically bonded interfacial bridge will reduce W/Cu interfacial thermal resistance and improve composite thermal conductivity.
The Ni-rich interface will resist irradiation-induced microstructural degradation.
After high-heat-flux and ion-irradiation exposure, the Ni-modified W–Cu composite will retain higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically undergo significant phase separation and interfacial void formation during high-temperature or irradiation cycling.
Phase separation and interfacial void formation degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
The processing temperature, heating rate, and duration must be controlled to create a transient liquid without excessive intermetallic growth.
The proposed interface will remain beneficial under high heat flux and Ar+, He+, or other ion irradiation relevant to W plasma-facing and Cu cooling components.
The quantitative conductivity improvement, optimal Ni loading, and optimal processing parameters remain unknown pending experimental calibration.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing identically processed Ni-added and Ni-free W–Cu composites before and after thermal cycling and irradiation.
Failure of the Ni-added specimens to show statistically improved interfacial integrity or measurably higher post-treatment thermal conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.
